Predicting F1 Lap Time and Tyre Degradation

Machine learning on FastF1 race data, 2022 to 2025. All models implemented from scratch with NumPy and pandas.
NameVeer MehtaRoll No.23BCP090
CollegePDPUSemester7
SubjectMachine Learning LabProfessorDr. Himanshu Gajera
Date28 October 2026

1. Problem

As a tyre wears, a car gets slower, so teams need to know how much time a driver loses per lap of tyre age to decide when to pit. We predict how many seconds slower or faster a lap will be than the race's field-median lap, from the tyre, the fuel load, the weather, the car's recent form and the traffic. Degradation appears as the effect of tyre age once fuel burn is removed.

2. Data

Lap-by-lap timing, tyre and weather data from the FastF1 API for 92 races from 2022 to 2025. We keep dry, green-flag laps only: lap 1, pit laps, safety car, virtual safety car and yellow-flag laps, rain, deleted laps and laps slower than 104% of the driver's best are removed. That leaves 70,830 laps from 90 races. Fuel burn (about 2.95 s over a full race) is estimated from the data.

3. Method

Target. Lap time minus the race's field-median lap time, in seconds. This removes circuit length and year-to-year pace differences.

Features. Tyre compound and age (with non-linear terms and an age-by-compound interaction), lap number and race fraction as a fuel proxy, stint, track and air temperature, humidity, wind, driver and team form (their average pace over earlier races only), traffic (gaps to the cars ahead and behind and position at the end of the previous lap), and field context (the field's pace trend and laps since the last safety car or yellow flag).

Model. Gradient boosting with regression trees, written from scratch (Friedman's LAD-TreeBoost generalised to a pinball, or quantile, loss). Features are binned into histograms; each round fits a tree to the negative gradient of the loss, with row and column subsampling, and each leaf is set to the quantile of the residuals it contains. At the median this is the absolute-error loss, which is robust to traffic and mistakes. Quantile versions at 5% and 95%, calibrated with split conformal prediction, give 90% prediction intervals. Ridge regression and least squares are also implemented in NumPy. Against XGBoost on the same split the implementation differs by under 0.002 s in MAE.

Three tiers. The pre-lap model uses everything known at the start of the lap except the driver's own previous lap times. The pre-stint model adds how the driver went in the earlier stints of the same race (their mean pace, the pace at the end of the previous stint and its length). The live model also adds the driver's previous clean laps in the same stint, like a pit-wall forecast.

Baselines. The median lap; persistence (the driver's last 3 laps averaged); Formula A, the structure of an online degradation calculator (base plus compound, track temperature, air temperature and abrasiveness factors times laps) with constants fitted to our data; Formula B, Formula A plus fuel and form; and ridge regression on the same features as the pre-lap model.

Validation. Training on 2022 to 2024 (52,092 laps, 66 races) and testing on all of 2025 (18,738 laps, 24 unseen races). Mixed-year 5-fold cross-validation by race, where each fold holds out about 20% of every year's races, and leave-one-year-out. Laps from one race are never split between training and test.

5. Tyre degradation and circuit characteristics

The lap-level model predicts lap time, so tyre age is only one of several effects it learns, and comparing different drivers and stints confounds the compound with car, driver and strategy. Asking it what-if questions, such as a soft tyre running 30 laps in a late stint, also falls outside the data it has seen, which flattened the compound differences in an early version of our app. We therefore estimate degradation directly: every stint is compared only with itself (stint fixed effects) after removing fuel burn, so driver pace, car and strategy cancel out.

Degradation model. A least-squares regression written in NumPy explains the within-stint lap-time change by tyre age for each compound (linear and quadratic terms), its interaction with track temperature, and its interaction with circuit characteristics.

We also tried flexible piecewise-linear curve shapes, which can show a flat start or a late cliff. Judged by how well the curve reproduces the observed average tyre-age curves on held-out races, the parabola was best (curve error 0.136 s on unseen 2025 stints against 0.145 to 0.147 s for the flexible shapes), so it is kept; the data do not support a cliff or a flat start beyond what it captures. Figure 4 compares the observed averages with the model. The shaded bands in Figure 3 are 95% intervals from resampling whole races.

Circuit characteristics. For each of the 25 circuits we measured 13 characteristics from the telemetry of the fastest race lap: lap length, average speed, top speed, slowest-corner speed, the shares of the lap at full throttle and on the brakes, the number of heavy braking zones, mean cornering load in g, the share of the lap above 2.5 g, the numbers of slow, medium and fast corners, and elevation change per kilometre. Which ones to include was decided by cross-validation inside the training seasons only.

Figure 5. Correlation of each circuit characteristic with measured degradation severity across 25 circuits (selected characteristic in red).
  • Compounds separate clearly. Soft tyres lose 0.067 s per lap, medium 0.050 and hard 0.038, so soft degrades about 1.7 times faster than hard, and the model reproduces this (0.064, 0.049, 0.038).
  • One circuit characteristic held up. Cross-validation on the training seasons selected elevation change per kilometre (correlation 0.59 with measured circuit severity). Adding it improves the held-out stint slope correlation from 0.35 to 0.37. Using all 13 characteristics or each circuit's own history does not help: within-stint R² 0.30 and 0.19 against 0.31.
  • Circuit degradation is not predictable from these characteristics alone. Predicting a circuit's severity from all 13 gives R² -0.17 on circuits left out. Tyre allocation, weather and race incidents also matter, and a circuit's severity is not stable from year to year (correlation between consecutive seasons: 0.73, 0.41, 0.15).
  • In the lap-level model it helps tyre behaviour, not lap time. Adding elevation change raises the stint slope correlation of the pre-lap gradient boosting model from 0.55 to 0.57, but its lap-time error is not better (MAE 0.465 s without, 0.468 s with).

6. The app

A Streamlit app with four tabs makes the models explorable. Predictor draws the degradation curves for the three compounds at any circuit and track temperature, with 95% bands and a second view that adds fuel burn, so lap times can fall while the tyre wears. Race explorer plots the real stints of any driver in any race from 2022 to 2025 against what the model expects. Circuits ranks the 25 circuits by predicted tyre loss. Model shows the scores from this report.

Figure 6. Predictor tab: curves and 95% bands for the three compounds at Bahrain, with the circuit profile measured from telemetry.
Figure 7. Race explorer tab: one driver's real stints (dots) against the degradation model (line). Single stints are noisy and the model describes the typical case.

7. Validation checks

  • No leakage. A model trained on shuffled targets scores R² 0.00 and MAE 0.87, the same as the baseline.
  • Not a lucky season. Leave-one-year-out gives similar errors for every year (below), so regulation changes do not break the model.
  • Overfitting. Pre-lap train MAE 0.374 against test 0.468; live 0.261 against 0.294.
  • Not by chance. Resampling the 24 test races 1,000 times, the pre-lap MAE has a 95% interval of 0.43 to 0.52 s and beats Formula B by 0.12 s (0.08 to 0.16) in every resample.
  • Intervals. The calibrated 90% prediction intervals cover 93% (pre-lap) and 93% (pre-stint) and 93% (live) of 2025 laps, with mean widths of 2.2 s, 2.1 s and 1.5 s.

8. Limitations

  • A single lap carries about 0.33 s of random noise from traffic and mistakes, so lap-level R² has a ceiling near 0.9 for any model; most pre-lap error is each driver's race-specific offset, which no pre-lap information reveals.
  • Circuit characteristics are measured once per circuit from one fast lap (the latest season available), so layout changes between seasons are ignored, and with only 25 circuits their effects cannot be separated reliably.
  • The target is relative to the race's field-median lap, which comes from the session itself, not from a separate forecast.
  • Compound differences in the average curves are small next to circuit, fuel and traffic effects, and drivers manage their tyres, so the model captures typical behaviour, not a strategy decision.
  • The live model is mostly persistence: the plain last-3-lap average already reaches R² 0.72.
  • Some design choices (the lap filter and feature set) were made while looking at 2025 results, so the 2025 holdout is slightly optimistic; cross-validation is the better estimate.

9. Conclusion

A from-scratch gradient boosting model predicts lap time relative to the field with MAE 0.468 s (R² 0.66) using only information available before the lap, against 0.875 s for a naive baseline and 0.588 s for a fitted formula, and reproduces real tyre-age curves on unseen races. Knowing how the driver went in earlier stints cuts the error to 0.437 s (R² 0.70). With the driver's recent laps, error drops to 0.294 s, 20% better than simple persistence.
